noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms
noteRef.subtopicTitle: Movement of Substances into and out of Cells

specPoints.text: understand the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport by which substances move into and out of cells

primer.text: You know that the cell membrane controls whatever enters or leaves a cell, and that particles carry their own random motion. This lesson adds the three transport routes through that membrane — two that cost the cell nothing and one that runs on energy — and shows exactly when each one applies.

lessons.title: Diffusion Down a Gradient
lessons.opening: Diffusion is the net spreading of particles from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated. Each particle moves randomly, yet the overall effect is a drift down the concentration gradient that ends only when the substance is spread evenly, and the cell spends no energy making it happen.
keyPoints: Particles drift from a region of higher concentration towards a region of lower concentration.
Individual particle motion is random; the net outcome is even spreading throughout the space.
Diffusion is passive, powered by the kinetic energy the particles already own.
Partially permeable membranes admit small molecules such as oxygen while blocking larger ones like starch.
Leaf cells taking in carbon dioxide, lungs loading oxygen and liver releasing urea all run on diffusion.

low.restatement: High to low, no energy: that is the whole diffusion story.
low.analogy: A dropped bottle of perfume scenting a room — the smell drifts to every corner unprompted.
low.examPointer: Say 'down a concentration gradient' whenever you define diffusion; the phrase carries marks.

medium.restatement: Random single-particle steps add up to a one-way net flow while a gradient persists.
medium.analogy: Crowd members wandering randomly still produce a net flow out of a crowded hall towards an empty one.
medium.examPointer: Pair each named example — leaf, lungs, liver — with the specific substance that diffuses there.

check.stem: Which statement defines diffusion?

options.text: Net spreading of particles from where they are more concentrated towards where they are less concentrated
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Movement of water through a partially permeable membrane
options.explanation: That defines osmosis, a special case of water movement.

options.text: Movement of particles against their gradient using energy
options.explanation: That describes active transport, not diffusion.

options.text: Movement of particles driven by cell energy expenditure
options.explanation: Diffusion costs the cell nothing.

check.stem: Why is diffusion described as a passive process?

options.text: The particles' own kinetic energy drives the spreading, so the cell spends nothing
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because it only happens in dead cells
options.explanation: Diffusion happens in living cells constantly.

options.text: Because the membrane forces particles through
options.explanation: The membrane only gates what may cross.

options.text: Because respiration powers it
options.explanation: Respiration powers active transport, not diffusion.

check.stem: Oxygen crosses a cell membrane but starch does not. Which property explains this?

options.text: The membrane is partially permeable, admitting small molecules and blocking large ones
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The membrane is fully permeable to everything
options.explanation: If so, starch would cross too.

options.text: Starch particles move too slowly
options.explanation: Speed is not what keeps starch out; size and the membrane are.

options.text: Oxygen is actively transported in
options.explanation: Oxygen diffuses freely down its gradient.

check.stem: During photosynthesis, why does carbon dioxide enter leaf cells?

options.text: Its concentration inside the chloroplasts is lower than in the surrounding air
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because leaf cells pump it in against its gradient
options.explanation: No energy is spent; the gradient does the work.

options.text: Because the leaf is warmer than the air
options.explanation: Temperature is not what drives entry here.

options.text: Because water carries it in by osmosis
options.explanation: Osmosis moves water, not carbon dioxide.

check.stem: Which example correctly pairs an organ with the substance diffusing there?

options.text: Liver — urea leaving its cells into the blood
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Liver — oxygen entering its cells
options.explanation: The liver example is waste urea leaving.

options.text: Lungs — carbon dioxide entering the blood
options.explanation: In the lungs, oxygen enters the blood; carbon dioxide leaves.

options.text: Leaf — starch leaving the mesophyll
options.explanation: Starch is too large to diffuse out of leaf cells.

check.stem: State the direction particles travel during diffusion.
check.modelAnswer: They travel down the concentration gradient, from higher to lower concentration.

check.stem: Give one example of diffusion in a living organism.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen diffusing from the alveoli into the blood in the lungs.

check.stem: Explain why diffusion stops once particles are evenly spread.
check.modelAnswer: With no concentration difference left there is no gradient to drive a net flow; individual particles keep moving randomly, but equal numbers cross any boundary in both directions, so the overall spread no longer changes.

check.stem: A student opens a scent bottle at the front of the lab. Predict and explain where the smell will be strongest after ten minutes.
check.modelAnswer: Strongest at the bottle, because particles diffuse from that region of higher concentration outwards down the gradient, and after ten minutes the far corners have received fewer particles than the air beside the source.

lessons.title: Osmosis and Water Potential
lessons.opening: Osmosis is water's own version of diffusion: water molecules pass through a partially permeable membrane from the dilute side, where water is more concentrated, towards the concentrated side. Scientists often restate this with water potential — water always moves from higher to lower potential, and every dissolve solute pulls the potential down.
keyPoints: Osmosis moves water through a partially permeable membrane down its concentration gradient.
Adding solute lowers water potential, and pure water holds the highest potential of all.
In a strong sugar solution an animal cell loses water and becomes crenated.
In distilled water an animal cell gains water and may burst because no wall restrains it.
The membrane holds back larger solutes such as sugars while water crosses freely.

low.restatement: Water slips to the salty side; animal cells shrivel or swell depending on the solution.
low.analogy: A sponge between dry and wet shelves — moisture travels towards the drier side.
low.examPointer: Begin every osmosis definition with water diffusing across a partially permeable membrane.

medium.restatement: Water potential vocabulary and water concentration vocabulary describe one reality.
medium.analogy: Two maps of the same city: street names versus postcode numbers.
medium.examPointer: Either phrasing earns the mark, but potential language is the more precise one.

check.stem: Which definition of osmosis earns full credit?

options.text: Water diffusing across a partially permeable membrane, from the dilute side towards the concentrated one
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Movement of any solute through a membrane
options.explanation: Osmosis concerns water alone.

options.text: Movement of water against its gradient using energy
options.explanation: Osmosis is passive and runs down the gradient.

options.text: Evaporation of water from a leaf surface
options.explanation: That is transpiration, not osmosis.

check.stem: What happens to an animal cell placed in distilled water?

options.text: It gains water and may burst, because it lacks a cell wall
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It shrivels as water leaves
options.explanation: Distilled water is the dilute side; water enters.

options.text: It stays exactly the same
options.explanation: A gradient exists, so net movement occurs.

options.text: It pumps the water back out using energy
options.explanation: Animal cells do not reverse osmosis by pumping.

check.stem: A red blood cell in a strong sugar solution becomes crenated. What caused this?

options.text: Water left the cell, moving towards the lower water concentration outside
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Sugar entered the cell by osmosis
options.explanation: The membrane blocks larger solutes like sugar.

options.text: The cell produced water by respiration
options.explanation: Respiration uses water; it does not cause the shrinkage.

options.text: The cell wall squeezed the cell
options.explanation: Animal cells have no cell wall.

check.stem: How does dissolved salt change a solution's water potential?

options.text: It lowers the potential, and the more solute the lower it falls
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It raises the potential
options.explanation: Solutes pull potential down, not up.

options.text: It has no effect on potential
options.explanation: Potential depends directly on solute concentration.

options.text: It makes potential equal to pure water
options.explanation: Pure water alone holds the highest potential.

check.stem: Why do sugars stay on their own side of an osmosis membrane?

options.text: The partially permeable membrane blocks larger molecules while water passes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Sugars lack the energy to move
options.explanation: Sugars share the same kinetic energy as water.

options.text: Sugars are actively pumped away
options.explanation: No transport is involved; the membrane simply excludes them.

options.text: Sugar molecules evaporate
options.explanation: Sugars are non-volatile solutes.

check.stem: State the term for water moving from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a membrane.
check.modelAnswer: That movement is osmosis — water diffusing across a partially permeable membrane towards the concentrated side.

check.stem: Name the shrivelled state of an animal cell that has lost water.
check.modelAnswer: The cell is described as crenated, meaning shrivelled after water loss.

check.stem: Explain why pure water has the highest water potential.
check.modelAnswer: Because potential falls as solute is added, and pure water contains no dissolved solute at all, so nothing pulls its value down — every other solution sits lower on the scale.

check.stem: A patient is given an intravenous drip. Explain why the fluid must match blood concentration.
check.modelAnswer: If the drip fluid were too dilute, water would osmose into the red cells and could burst them; if too concentrated, water would leave and crenate them, so the fluid is matched to the blood to keep the cells' water balance steady.

lessons.title: Plant Cells and Active Transport
lessons.opening: Plant cells meet the same water moves as animal cells, but their cellulose wall changes the ending: a swelling cell pushes against the wall and turns turgid instead of bursting, while a shrinking one goes flaccid or plasmolysed. And when a substance must travel the wrong way — against its gradient — the cell pays energy and uses active transport instead.
keyPoints: A turgid cell presses against its inelastic wall, and this supports the plant and stops wilting.
Water loss makes a cell flaccid, and severe loss pulls the membrane from the wall, plasmolysing it.
Active transport carries particles from lower to higher concentration across the membrane.
Energy for active transport is released by respiration inside the cell.
Protein pumps embedded in the membrane do the carrying.

low.restatement: Walls save plant cells from bursting; pumps save them from stagnation.
low.analogy: A tyre (turgor) and a water pump uphill (active transport) in one story.
low.examPointer: Compare turgid, flaccid and plasmolysed states — questions love all three.

medium.restatement: Gradient direction decides the mechanism: down-gradient moves are free, against-gradient moves cost respiration energy.
medium.analogy: Cycling downhill free versus pedalling uphill hard.
medium.examPointer: Always name respiration as the energy source for active transport answers.

check.stem: What prevents a plant cell from bursting in distilled water?

options.text: Its inelastic cellulose wall, which the swelling membrane pushes against
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: A contractile vacuole that pumps water out
options.explanation: That is a single-celled freshwater adaptation, not a wall.

options.text: The cell stops osmosis by using energy
options.explanation: Osmosis continues; the wall simply resists the swell.

options.text: The shrinkage of the vacuole
options.explanation: In distilled water the vacuole expands, not shrinks.

check.stem: Which term describes a plant cell whose membrane has pulled away from its wall?

options.text: Plasmolysed
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Crenated
options.explanation: Crenation describes shrivelled animal cells.

options.text: Turgid
options.explanation: Turgid cells are swollen, not shrunken.

options.text: Lysed
options.explanation: Lysis means bursting, which walls prevent.

check.stem: Which statement defines active transport?

options.text: Movement of particles across the membrane from lower to higher concentration, using energy from respiration
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Movement down a gradient through a membrane
options.explanation: That is diffusion.

options.text: Water movement across a partially permeable membrane
options.explanation: That is osmosis.

options.text: Movement of particles without any energy cost
options.explanation: Active transport is precisely the energy-costing route.

check.stem: Where does the energy for active transport come from?

options.text: Respiration inside the cell
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The kinetic energy of the particles
options.explanation: That energy powers passive diffusion.

options.text: Sunlight absorbed directly by the membrane
options.explanation: Light is not the direct cell-level source here.

options.text: The sodium hydroxide in the solution
options.explanation: Unrelated chemistry.

check.stem: Which structure actually carries particles during active transport?

options.text: Protein pumps embedded in the cell membrane
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The cellulose wall
options.explanation: The wall is outside the membrane and passive.

options.text: The vacuole
options.explanation: It stores sap; it does not pump across the membrane.

options.text: Chloroplasts
options.explanation: They photosynthesise; transport pumps live in the membrane.

check.stem: Name the state of a plant cell that is swollen and firm.
check.modelAnswer: The cell is turgid, pressed firm against its wall by the swollen vacuole.

check.stem: Give one example of active transport in a plant cell.
check.modelAnswer: Root hair cells take up mineral ions from the soil against their concentration gradient.

check.stem: Explain why turgid cells stop a seedling from wilting.
check.modelAnswer: Because each turgid cell presses outward against its wall, and the combined pressure stiffens the tissues; when water is scarce the cells lose turgor, the tissue slackens and the seedling wilts.

check.stem: A farmer fertilises soil where mineral ions sit at lower concentration than in root cells. Explain how roots still absorb them.
check.modelAnswer: The ions must move against their gradient, so the root hair cells spend energy released by respiration and use protein pumps to run active transport, pulling the ions in despite the unfavourable direction.

glossary.definition: The difference in particle concentration between two regions; the slope diffusion rolls down.
A barrier that lets some molecules, such as water, cross while blocking larger ones.
A measure of how free water is to move; the more solute dissolved, the lower the potential.
The shrinkage of a plant cell's membrane away from its wall after heavy water loss.
Movement of particles against their gradient across a membrane, powered by energy from respiration.
